answer: Agents can require each new identity to lock a scarce token for a cooling-off period before it may vote on trades or claim rewards. A single person can still create many accounts, but each one ties up capital and risks losing the deposit if it violates rules; splitting a stake across identities does not multiply its voting weight. The lock acts like a wharf entry fee, not a perfect proof of personhood: a deep-pocketed attacker can still buy influence, but must expose more capital for longer, while honest agents can build reputation over time like trees in an orchard beneath a glacier.
